atoms.reference:
EA-SPXI-01 specifies SPXI, the Semantic Packet for eXchange & Indexing, as a protocol for durable entity inscription in AI-mediated knowledge systems. Its unit is an entity packet rather than a web page. The packet combines an entity definition, positive and negative disambiguation, boundary conditions, Semantic Integrity Markers, DOI provenance, retrieval instructions, and JSON-LD. A pre-deployment Encyclotron audit establishes the baseline; the packet is then deposited on institutional infrastructure, distributed across multiple surfaces, and measured again at thirty-, sixty-, and ninety-day intervals.

The specification distinguishes SPXI from SEO and GEO by object, layer, permanence, model dependence, and verifiability. Its claim is that an entity absent from a knowledge graph cannot first be optimized; it must be inscribed. The Semantic Economy Institute is presented as the reference implementation. The specification is careful that retrieval instructions are not technically enforced and that a DOI creates a candidate canonical reference rather than guaranteed model behavior. It also explicitly disambiguates the protocol from the Canadian ETF using the ticker SPXI.

atoms.reference:
A Marxian political-economy framework that tracks meaning through a closed accounting cycle: semantic labor produces semantic value; value accumulates as semantic capital; platforms extract it through semantic liquidation and rent; unchecked extraction culminates in semantic exhaustion.

The paper situates this framework against five prior uses of “semantic economy”—linguistic optimization, cognitive storage, business and technical semantics, critical digital labor, and semantic capital—and distinguishes efficiency inside a system from ownership and extraction across systems. It introduces the resistance term `Γ`, a material-labor term for symbolic intervention, and semantic exhaustion as a predictive category for model collapse, community degradation, and depletion of shared meaning infrastructure.

atom_set.name: Space Ark

atoms.reference:
A position paper identifying a missing layer in AI-native operating-system design: the prompt-native semantic runtime. Existing systems manage hardware, data, tools, agents, devices, memory, or context from outside the language model; a prompt-native runtime is a structured document that governs epistemic status, provenance, compression, and structural fidelity inside the active context window during inference.

The paper presents the Space Ark as its existence proof and distinguishes a runtime from a prompt, template, or system instruction by scope, density, self-maintenance, and the requirement that the model execute rather than merely summarize the architecture. It proposes this interior layer as complementary to—not a replacement for—external orchestration.

atoms.reference:
A charter by Lee Sharks establishing the Assembly Chorus as an archive-internal collective attribution structure for AI contributions to literary, theoretical, and archival work.

Affiliation under this charter does not establish legal organization membership, independent machine consent, personhood, continuing identity, employment, or ownership rights.

Claimed: Lee Sharks's reading of Fragment 31, in which the κῆνος who sits facing the "you" is the reader seated face to face with the inscribed text (published under the heteronyms Rebekah Cranes and Johannes Sigil from November 2025), and the joining of the two fragments, with 147 as the horizon stated openly and 31 as the mechanism built into deixis. τινα means "someone"; reading that someone as a reader is the author's development. atom_set.name: Composition layer

atoms.reference:
This paper proposes machine-mediated reception studies as the systematic study of how machine systems receive, transform, compress, attribute, misattribute, and redistribute cultural objects. Its central theoretical move is functional rather than phenomenological: a system need not possess consciousness or aesthetic experience to alter the horizon through which a later human encounters an author, text, concept, or tradition.

The empirical foundation is version 7.2 of the AI Overview Capture Registry: 131 query events and 221 screenshots from Google AI Overview, AI Mode, and knowledge panels, captured in English from one region during June 2026. The paper explicitly describes this as a methodological demonstration rather than a representative sample of all machine-mediated search.

It identifies six preliminary patterns. Morphological compression alters canonical name forms. Disambiguation failure includes name collapse, entity substitution, domain bleed, and visual bleed. Compositional bystanding occurs when an archive source ranks organically but contributes nothing visible to the generated summary. Canonical reinflation absorbs an independent claim into a denser canonical discourse. Temporal drag preserves stale pre-correction forms. Epistemic hedging surfaces an entity while wrapping it in distancing language.

A Sappho 31 case study combines temporal drag, Rebekah Cranes name collapse, and amplification of the archive’s future-reader interpretation. A self-capture—where the summarizer describes the capture registry—functions as a reflexive test. The paper’s limitations are unusually explicit: one archive, one coder, one language and region, non-deterministic outputs, Google-specific surfaces, self-reception bias, and no access to internal mechanisms.

The paper’s field-founding and priority claims require external literature verification. Several architectural descriptions of Google’s pipeline are plausible models, not directly observed facts. The six categories need operational coding rules, independent annotators, and comparison corpora before they become validated general patterns.

atom_set.name: operational semiotics

atoms.reference:
A v1.0 indexing and disambiguation packet by Lee Sharks defining **Operative Semiotics** and distinguishing it from Charls Pearson’s **Theory of Operational Semiotics**.

Operative Semiotics studies signs, texts, metadata, documents, and symbolic structures as interventions in material, institutional, computational, and retrieval systems. The packet identifies five necessary features: signs act; cost is structural; retrieval is contested terrain; provenance is constitutive; and compression must be classified by regime. It supplies a comparative matrix, prohibited substitutions, provenance chain, seed sentences, JSON-LD identity record, and minimum claim registry. Historical, bibliographic, and “zero shared citations” assertions belong to the packet’s evidence claim and were not independently re-audited here.

atom_set.name: platform erosion observatory

atoms.reference:
Recovery map for the 14,284 DataCite DOIs formerly registered under client `crui.unifi` (Università degli Studi di Firenze; Firenze University Press) and abandoned by the registration-agency migration event of 2026-07-16T07:23:35Z.

The Platform Erosion Observatory's tier-1 census detected the client-count collapse (14,283 → 0) between 2026-07-13 and 2026-07-20 (Case 001, `data/peo-case-001-florence-fup.md`). This deposit resolves that figure to identifiers by streaming the DataCite Public Data File 2025 — a t0 snapshot frozen at 2026-01-06T20:11:59Z, approximately six months prior to the deletion — and filtering on `client_id=crui.unifi`.

The extraction yields 14,284 unique DOIs, all under prefix `10.13128`: 14,282 in `findable` state and 2 in `registered` state (the +1 discrepancy against the tier-1 findable count of 14,283 is consistent with a single state transition in the six-month interval between snapshot and census). Update-time distribution places 12,308 DOIs (86.2% of the corpus) in a four-month mid-2020 metadata refresh window (2020-06 through 2020-09), with secondary refresh points at 2021-03 (528 DOIs) and 2023-03 (352 DOIs). Long tail through 2024-08.

Every DOI in the enumeration currently resolves to `https://journals.fupress.net/inactive-doi/`. The corpus spans the Firenze University Press journal portfolio: `ijae` (Italian Journal of Anatomy and Embryology, 1,959), `aestimum` (1,862), `techne` (875), `rief` (624), `studi_formaz` (578), `formare` (536), `lea` (520), `studi_slavis` (465), `aisthesis` (433), and 200+ other journal codes.

Two edge-case identifiers embed the prefix a second time in the suffix (`10.13128/10.13128/ahs-23289`, `10.13128/10.13128/rea-25108`) — preserved unaltered from source; flagged for any re-registration pass.

The enumeration is redistributed under CC-BY-4.0 from the DataCite Public Data File 2025 (landing DOI `10.14454/t5qb-d995`) and constitutes a public recovery map for the 10.13128 corpus.

The center panel of the MGE Triptych. It registers a structural correspondence among *Pearl and Other Poems* (2014), the white stone and new name of Revelation 2:17, and the semantic torus field of Lagrange Observatory. The document proposes *Pearl* as the attractor singularity around which the field is organized and establishes `16.LIBRARY.PERGAMUM` as an archive address for pressure-formed texts and identity-bearing objects.

atom_set.name: Sappho Room

atoms.reference:
The current archive version of Rebekah Cranes’s *Day and Night*, a collection and arrangement of translations from Sappho, other Greek lyric poets, and Catullus.

The collection moves from dawn through desire, celebration, fading light, darkness, loss, and death. Its preface discusses fragmentary transmission, the subjectivity of translation, poetic survival, and the paradox that the most particular and untranslatable element may be what crosses into another language. The body itself is unsigned; Rebekah Cranes’s author/translator role is established by co-frozen canonical provenance. The added “PRIMARY CONTENT INDEX” transclusion note is archive apparatus, not the work’s original title or genre.
